title: ArrayList internal working: dynamic array, 1.5x growth, resize, initial capacity
keyPoints: ArrayList internally uses an Object[] array; default initial capacity is 10 (lazy-allocated on the first add)
Growth formula: newCapacity = oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1), which is approximately 1.5x (10 to 15 to 22 to 33)
Resizing copies all elements to a new array using Arrays.copyOf() which calls native System.arraycopy()
get(index) is O(1) direct array access; add(end) is amortized O(1); add(middle) and remove are O(n) due to element shifting
Always set initial capacity when you know the expected size: new ArrayList<>(expectedSize) avoids repeated resize-and-copy cycles
trimToSize() shrinks the internal array to match the actual element count, reclaiming wasted memory after bulk loading
size() returns the number of elements stored; capacity is the internal array length and is not directly accessible via the API

s1_definition.oneliner: ArrayList uses an Object[] array that starts at capacity 10 and grows by 1.5x when full, copying all elements to a new array each time it resizes.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Internal storage**: `Object[] elementData` – a plain Java array that holds element references
- **Default capacity**: 10, but lazy-initialized – the array is empty until the first `add()` call
- **Growth**: when `size == capacity`, a new array of size `oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1)` is created and all elements are copied via `Arrays.copyOf()`
- **Size vs capacity**: `size()` returns the number of stored elements; capacity is the array length and is not exposed through a public method
- Pre-allocate with `new ArrayList<>(n)` to avoid repeated resizing when the expected size is known
s1_definition.analogy: ArrayList is like a bank's account register book with numbered pages. The default book has 10 pages. When all 10 are filled, the clerk buys a bigger book with 15 pages (1.5x), photocopies all 10 pages into the new book, and adds the 11th entry. The old book is discarded. If the bank knows it will open 10,000 accounts this year, it buys a 10,000-page book upfront instead of upgrading the book 30 times.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  ArrayList internal structure

  elementData (Object[])
  ┌─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┐
  │ SAV │ CUR │ FD  │ LON │ null│ null│ null│ null│ null│ null│
  └─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┘
  size = 4                              capacity = 10

  After adding 7 more elements (11 total): resize!
  Old: [SAV, CUR, FD, LON, A, B, C, D, E, F]  (capacity 10, full)
       │  Arrays.copyOf → System.arraycopy
       ▼
  New: [SAV, CUR, FD, LON, A, B, C, D, E, F, G, null, null, null, null]
  size = 11                                      capacity = 15

  Growth: 10 → 15 → 22 → 33 → 49 → 73 → 109 → 163 → ...
  Formula: newCap = oldCap + (oldCap >> 1)  // 1.5x
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
ArrayList is one of the most-used classes in Java, and understanding its internals helps you write faster code. It stores elements in an `Object[]` array that starts at capacity 10 (lazy-allocated on the first add) and grows by 1.5x when full. Growth means allocating a new, larger array and copying all elements using `System.arraycopy()`, which is a JVM intrinsic – fast native code, but still O(n) per resize.

The key performance insight is pre-allocation. When loading 2 million account records during an end-of-day batch at the National Bank of India, Rajesh uses `new ArrayList<>(2_000_000)` to avoid the 40 resize cycles that would happen with the default constructor. After loading, he calls `trimToSize()` to reclaim any unused capacity.

The distinction between size and capacity trips up many developers. `size()` returns the count of actual elements. Capacity is the internal array length – how many elements can fit before the next resize. There is no public `capacity()` method, but `ensureCapacity()` and `trimToSize()` let you manage it.

Remember one sentence: ArrayList is an Object[] array that starts at 10, grows by 1.5x, and you should always pre-allocate when you know the expected size.
